Sessions.Name: Sky session protocol design
Sessions.LastPrompt: explain the link protocol we built
Sessions.Recap: We didn't build a link protocol — that idea got designed, then discarded once you said you read the brief on the phone first. What shipped is a file queue. Worth being precise about, because the two solve the same problem in opposite ways. ## Why the protocol died `skysession://resume/<id>` would have been a Windows URL scheme registered under `HKCU\Software\Classes`, so a click in anything that renders links launches the app. Two things killed it for the brief: - **Chat UIs sanitize it away.** Markdown renderers allowlist `http`/`https`/`mailto`; a custom scheme comes out as dead grey text, same as in a GitHub README. - **A phone has no Windows handler.** You read the brief on the train. There's nothing there to receive the tap. ## What we built instead The channel that already existed only ran one way. `kk-sessions-dump` writes `sessions.json` into `C:\Users\kk\Code\sky-session-claude` at 06:45; Dispatch's Linux sandbox has that folder mounted and reads it. Everything you decided at 7am, you carried back and re-typed. The inbox is the return leg: ``` 06:45 host ── sessions.json ──▶ Dispatch (sandbox) "here's what's unfinished" 07:12 host ◀── commands.json ── Dispatch (sandbox) "resume 1, tick off 3, drop 4" 07:15 host SessionCli inbox --run terminals open ``` You reply *in the brief*, in words. Dispatch writes the file. A task fires every five minutes and runs it. ```json { "issuedAt": "2026-08-23T07:12:00+01:00", "source": "dispatch", "commands": [ { "action": "resume", "id": "abc1234" }, { "action": "done", "id": "def5678" }, { "action": "new", "in": "C:\\Users\\kk\\Code\\address-vault" } ] } ``` **A folder beats both a link and a port because there's nothing to defend.** No listener, no token, no firewall rule, nothing a site you're browsing can reach — the only writers are the sandbox that already has the mount and processes already on this machine. And it works from a phone with no route to your desktop at all, because the decision rides back in a file rather than over a wire. Since the caller isn't in the room, three rules: | Guarantee | Mechanism | |---|---| | Runs once | Queue moves to `commands.last.json` *before* results are written | | Never runs late | Older than `--max-age` (120 min) → refused whole, moved aside | | Never trusted | No `--force`/`--trust`; `fork` and `trust` aren't actions; `new` only into folders that already have sessions | Each command runs through the verb you'd have typed, so it inherits every refusal already in the tool rather than re-deciding against a second, worse copy — that's why queuing a restart of the session running the queue gets *"it is the session this command is running in"* for free. ## Where the protocol stands Not built. Still the right answer for the half you were skeptical about at the start — you at the desk, a locally-rendered `brief.html`, one click instead of a reply. Local files have no sanitizer and no sandbox, and Chrome asks once and remembers. It's a registry key, a URI parser, and a route into the single-instance app — and it would feed this same inbox rather than being a second path. Say the word and it's an afternoon.

Sessions.LastPrompt: i want to build the protocol but lets briefstorm doube check the details. ask questions pls
Sessions.Recap: I read the repo state first so the questions are real ones. Here's what exists today (from the last two commits): - **Out:** `kk-sessions-dump` daily at 06:45 → `sessions.json` in the repo folder, which the brief's sandbox reads. - **In:** `kk-sessions-inbox` every 5 min, interactive → `SessionCli inbox --run commands.json`, forgiving parser, three gates (move-before-write, `--max-age 120`, no `--force`/`--trust`/`fork`, `new` only into a folder with existing sessions). - **Back:** `commands.json` → `commands.last.json`, results → `commands-result.json`. Gaps I can see in that as a *protocol* rather than a feature: 1. **The return leg has no reader.** `commands-result.json` is written and nothing ever opens it. Tomorrow's brief reads `sessions.json` only — so "did the 7:05 queue actually run?" is unanswerable, including when it was refused whole for age. 2. **`sessions.json` is stale the moment the inbox acts.** It's dumped at 06:45; the inbox resumes two sessions at 07:10 and the folder still describes the world before that. 3. **A half-written queue is eaten.** The sandbox writes `commands.json` non-atomically; if the task fires mid-write, the parse fails and the file is *moved aside* — the decisions are gone and the brief will never know it. Same for a second queue written before the task fires: it clobbers the first. 4. **No version, no per-command id.** Result items are keyed by `SessionId`, so two commands on one session collapse, and there's no way to reject a file written by a newer brief. 5. **Who teaches the brief?** `source: "dispatch"` points at something outside this repo. The queue format lives in a C# parser and a README section; the writer is an agent somewhere else with no schema to check itself against. Now the questions I actually need answered:

Sessions.Name: Evaluate salary versus pension benefits trade-off
Sessions.LastPrompt: 3. no need, assume I will have to set it up on my own. 4. not 4 options just explain how can i get it on my own.
Sessions.Recap: I read the FAQ and ran the numbers through `src/lib/faq.js` on the page's default scenario (born 1985, joined 2012, salary $90,755 in 2026, retire at 60, 4.5% discount rate). Here's what I found. ## 1. It isn't $5,000 — it's ~$21,000, unless your discount rate is doing the work On defaults, `equivalentSalary` returns: | | | |---|---| | Pensionable salary | $90,755 | | − your contribution (9.2%) | $8,334 | | = cash you keep | $82,421 | | + PV of this year's credit | $29,608 | | **= equivalent no-pension salary** | **$112,029** | | **Premium** | **$21,274 (23.4%)** | The premium only falls to ~$5,000 at a **discount rate of about 7.25%**. So if you're seeing $5k, either you raised that input, or your scenario is close to retirement (the PV of one year of credit shrinks as the payout window shortens). Sensitivity, retiring at 60: | Discount rate | Premium | |---|---| | 3.0% | $38,703 (43%) | | 4.5% (default) | $21,274 (23%) | | 6.0% | $10,736 (12%) | | 7.25% | ~$5,100 | | 8.0% | $2,627 (3%) | And that's the whole trap in one line: **7.25% nominal is an equity return, and you'd be assuming it with bond-like certainty.** The pension pays whether or not markets cooperate. Discounting an indexed, guaranteed, employer-backstopped stream at an equity rate is the standard way to talk yourself out of a good deal. A defensible rate for a guaranteed real stream is closer to 3–4.5%. ## 2. The bigger problem: the question is scoped to one year, and your real decision isn't This is the substantive gap I'd want to fix. `accrualValue()` prices *one year of credit* — and it's already a bit generous, because it values that year at your **best-five at retirement** ($145,762), which only materializes if you stay. Price the same year as "leave next year instead of this year" and it's worth $21,270, not $29,608. But the decision "should I take the other job" isn't a one-year trade. Leaving now also **freezes the best-five average under all 14 years you've already banked**. That's the number nothing on this page puts next to the salary question: | PV at 2026, 4.5% | | |---|---| | Leave now → deferred pension at 60 | $257,894 (credit 14, best-5 frozen at $83,127) | | Stay to 60 → Factor 90, unreduced | $977,057 (credit 33, best-5 $145,762) | | **Gap** | **$719,163** | | PV of the contributions you'd still pay | $140,954 | You spend $141k of your own money to buy $719k of pension. A $5,000 raise doesn't touch that; neither does $20,000. What *would* touch it is a genuinely different career, or an outside job that also has a DB plan. Caveat in the honest direction: that $719k assumes the new job has **no** pension at all. If it has a decent DC plan or another DB plan, most of the gap closes. ## 3. "How do I get the same pension if I leave?" Four real answers, roughly in descending order of how well they work: 1. **A reciprocal transfer agreement.** OPB has them with other Canadian public-sector plans (OMERS, HOOPP, OTPP, the federal plan, and others). Move to a participating employer within the window and your service can transfer, which un-freezes the base rather than stranding it. This is by far the best outcome and it's the single biggest omission in the current FAQ. *I'd want to verify the current list and the time limits before writing specifics into the page.* 2. **Another DB plan on its own terms.** No transfer, but a fresh 2%-ish indexed accrual starting from your new (higher) salary. You lose the retroactive uplift on the old service, keep the new accrual. 3. **A DC plan or group RRSP.** Match rates in the private sector are typically 4–6% of pay each side, against PSPP's 9.2% + 9.2%. Roughly half the money going in, and you carry the investment and longevity risk yourself. 4. **Fund it out of your own pocket.** This is where it gets sobering. Buying the future accrual alone as capital at 60 costs $1.4M–$1.8M depending on return assumption, which is 46–70% of current pay saved every year for 19 years. And an inflation-indexed life annuity — the thing that would actually replicate it — is essentially not sold in Canada anymore, so even with the capital you'd be self-insuring longevity. Two mechanical details also missing from the "what if I leave" answer: - **Commuted value transfers are capped.** The Income Tax Act maximum transfer value limits how much goes into a LIRA tax-sheltered; the excess is paid to you in cash and is **fully taxable in that year**. On a mid-career CV that can be a six-figure tax event. The current text calls the CV "roughly $X" with no hint of this. - **The PA stops, and a PAR may restore RRSP room.** Leaving frees up RRSP room going forward, which slightly offsets everything above. ## What I'd propose changing 1. **Reframe the salary question as two horizons.** Keep the current one-year equivalent salary, then add a second paragraph: "That is a one-year answer. Over the rest of your career the same question is worth $719,163." Reuse `leaving` and a new PV — the data is already computed. 2. **Add a discount-rate warning with teeth.** The existing note says the answer "moves a lot" with the rate. Say what the rate *means*: at 7%+ you're asserting you can earn equity returns with pension-like certainty. 3. **Flag when the outside job also has a pension** — one sentence, so nobody reads the $719k as unconditional. 4. **New FAQ: "If I leave, can I get this pension somewhere else?"** Covering the four options above. 5. **Add the ITA transfer cap** to the existing commuted-value note. Before I write any of it: **which scenario were you looking at when you saw $5,000?** If it's a raised discount rate, item 2 is the fix and it's the most important one. Also, do you want me to verify OPB's current reciprocal transfer agreements and the ITA maximum transfer value formula, or would you rather I write the text generically and leave the specifics for you to confirm?
